topic: European Trading Companies & Struggle for Supremacy

items.title: The Advent of Europeans & Order of Arrival
items.body:
**In one line** This topic is about which European powers came to India to trade, in what order, and why they crossed the oceans to get here.

**Why it is asked** APPSC loves the exact sequence of arrival and the founding years of the companies, because candidates mix up when a power *arrived* with when its *company* was formed.

**The story**

In the 15th century European traders wanted Indian **spices** (pepper, cinnamon, cloves) and fine cotton cloth. The land routes to the East ran through West Asia and were controlled by the **Ottoman Turks**, who charged heavy tolls. So Europeans looked for a **direct sea route** to India. Better ships and navigation, national rivalry, and a wish to spread Christianity pushed them to sail. The **Portuguese** came first in 1498, followed by the **Dutch**, the **English**, the **Danish** and finally the **French**.

**Picture it**

| Power | First factory | Year set up | Left India |
|---|---|---|---|
| Portuguese | Cochin | 1503 | 1961 |
| Dutch | Masulipatnam | 1605 | 1825 (ceded) |
| English | Surat | 1612–13 | 1947 |
| Danish | Tranquebar | 1620 | 1845 (sold) |
| French | Surat / Pondicherry | 1668 / 1674 | 1954 |

**Terms explained**

- **Factory** — not a modern mill, but a fortified *trading post and warehouse* where a company stored goods and housed its agents (called 'factors').
- **East India Company** — a joint-stock trading firm given a royal charter (a monopoly licence) to trade with the East.
- **Age of Discoveries** — the roughly 1450–1650 period when Europeans explored new sea routes to Asia and the Americas.

**Don't confuse** The *date a power first reached India* is different from the *year its trading company was founded*: the English company (1600) and the Dutch company (1602) were founded **before** the French company (1664), even though the French rose to prominence last.

**Remember it** 'Please Do Eat Delicious Food' = **P**ortuguese → **D**utch → **E**nglish → **D**anish → **F**rench (order of arrival).

**TL;DR**

- Motive: reach the spice and textile trade directly and bypass Ottoman-controlled land routes.
- Arrival order: Portuguese (1498) → Dutch → English → Danish → French.
- Portuguese were first to come and last to leave (Goa, 1961).
- Company founding years: English 1600, Dutch 1602, Danish 1616, French 1664.
keyPoints: Order of arrival: Portuguese → Dutch → English → Danish → French.
Motive: direct spice trade + bypassing Ottoman overland routes; the 'Age of Discoveries'.
Portuguese were the first to come (1498) and the last to leave (Goa, 1961).
Dutch first factory = Masulipatnam (1605); English first factory = Surat (1612–13).
English EIC chartered 1600, Dutch VOC 1602, French company 1664.
items.mnemonic: Arrival order 'Please Do Eat Delicious Food' = Portuguese, Dutch, English, Danish, French.

items.title: The Portuguese: Da Gama to the Blue Water Policy
items.body:
**In one line** How the Portuguese opened the sea route to India and became the first European power to build an Indian empire — from Vasco da Gama to the loss of Goa.

**Why it is asked** Names like Almeida and Albuquerque, the 'Blue Water Policy', and the Goa dates (1510 capture, 1530 capital, 1961 liberation) are classic one-mark facts.

**The story**

**Bartholomeu Diaz** rounded the southern tip of Africa (the **Cape of Good Hope**) in 1487, proving a sea route east was possible. In **1498 Vasco da Gama** sailed on and landed at **Calicut**, where the local ruler, the **Zamorin**, received him. The Portuguese built their first fort at **Cochin (1503)**. To control the trade they needed naval power, so the first viceroy **Francisco Almeida** followed the **Blue Water Policy** — be strong at sea rather than hold large land territories — and smashed a combined Egyptian–Arab–Zamorin fleet at the **Battle of Diu (1509)**. His successor **Alfonso de Albuquerque captured Goa from the Sultan of Bijapur in 1510** and is called the **real founder of Portuguese power in the East**. **Nino da Cunha** shifted the capital from Cochin to **Goa in 1530**. Over time Portuguese religious intolerance and piracy angered the Mughals, and the Dutch took their Malabar forts by 1663. Goa, Daman and Diu stayed Portuguese until India liberated them in **1961**.

**Picture it**

| Year | Event |
|---|---|
| 1487 | Diaz rounds the Cape of Good Hope |
| 1498 | Da Gama reaches Calicut (Zamorin) |
| 1503 | First fort at Cochin |
| 1509 | Battle of Diu — Almeida wins naval mastery |
| 1510 | Albuquerque takes Goa from Bijapur |
| 1530 | Goa made the capital (Nino da Cunha) |
| 1961 | Goa, Daman & Diu liberated by India |

**Terms explained**

- **Blue Water (Cartaz) Policy** — Almeida's idea of dominating the *sea* (blue water) and forcing Indian ships to buy a Portuguese pass (a **cartaz**) to sail safely.
- **Viceroy** — the king's deputy who rules a colony in his name.
- **Zamorin** — the title of the Hindu ruler of Calicut.

**Don't confuse** **Almeida** = Blue Water Policy and the Battle of Diu; **Albuquerque** = capture of Goa (1510) and 'real founder'. Students often swap the two.

**Remember it** Portuguese governors in order **A-A-N**: **A**lmeida (Blue Water) → **A**lbuquerque (Goa) → **N**ino da Cunha (capital to Goa).

**TL;DR**

- Da Gama reached Calicut (1498); first fort at Cochin (1503).
- Almeida: Blue Water Policy and the Battle of Diu (1509).
- Albuquerque took Goa (1510) from Bijapur — real founder of the eastern empire.
- Goa made capital 1530; Goa/Daman/Diu liberated 1961 — Portuguese last to leave.
keyPoints: Vasco da Gama reached Calicut in 1498 (Zamorin); first fort at Cochin, 1503.
Almeida began the Blue Water Policy; Battle of Diu (1509) secured naval supremacy.
Albuquerque captured Goa (1510) and is the real founder of Portuguese power in the East.
Goa became the Portuguese capital in 1530 (Nino da Cunha).
Goa, Daman and Diu were liberated in 1961 — Portuguese were last to leave.
items.mnemonic: Portuguese governors A-A-N: Almeida (Blue Water) → Albuquerque (Goa) → Nino da Cunha (capital to Goa).

items.title: Dutch, English, Danish & French Companies
items.body:
**In one line** The four companies that followed the Portuguese — Dutch, English, Danish and French — and where each set up its early trading posts.

**Why it is asked** First-factory sites and dates (Masulipatnam 1605, Surat 1612–13, Tranquebar 1620, Pondicherry 1674) and figures like Sir Thomas Roe and Dupleix are repeat prelims facts.

**The story**

The **Dutch** (their company, the VOC, formed in 1602) opened their first Indian factory at **Masulipatnam (1605)** on the Andhra coast and built **Fort Geldria at Pulicat**, the headquarters of 'Dutch Coromandel'. They cared most about the **East Indies (Indonesia)** spice islands, so their Indian trade (indigo, textiles, saltpetre) stayed secondary; the English finally broke Dutch power in India at the **Battle of Bedara (1759)** in Bengal. The **English** East India Company was chartered by **Queen Elizabeth I in 1600**; after the Battle of Swally it won a factory at **Surat (1612–13)**, and **Sir Thomas Roe** secured a trade *farman* (royal permit) from the Mughal emperor **Jahangir in 1615**. The English added **Madras (Fort St. George, 1639)** and **Bombay**, which came as **Catherine of Braganza's dowry (1661)** and passed to the Company in **1668**. The **Danish** company (1616) ran **Tranquebar (1620)**, near Tanjore, and later **Serampore** near Calcutta, and finally **sold its settlements to the British in 1845**. The **French** company, reorganised by **Colbert in 1664**, founded **Pondicherry (1674)** under **Francois Martin**; its governor **Dupleix (from 1742)** was the first to meddle in Indian succession disputes and raised **mixed Indian–French regiments** — a method the British later copied.

**Picture it**

| Company | Founded | First Indian factory | Note |
|---|---|---|---|
| Dutch (VOC) | 1602 | Masulipatnam (1605) | HQ Fort Geldria, Pulicat |
| English (EIC) | 1600 | Surat (1612–13) | Madras 1639, Bombay 1668 |
| Danish | 1616 | Tranquebar (1620) | Sold to British 1845 |
| French | 1664 | Surat (1668) / Pondicherry (1674) | Dupleix's interventions |

**Terms explained**

- **Farman** — a royal order or permit from the Mughal emperor; the English trade farman let them trade with light duties.
- **VOC** — the Dutch initials for the United (Dutch) East India Company.
- **Dowry** — property or money given with a bride; Bombay came to England this way from Portugal.

**Don't confuse** The **Battle of Colachel (1741)** was the **Dutch** being defeated by **Travancore** (king Marthanda Varma) — *not* by the British. It was the **Battle of Bedara (1759)** where the **English** defeated the Dutch in India.

**Missions in Danish towns** The Danes allowed missionaries the British would not. The **first Protestant mission in India**, the **Danish-Halle Mission** under **Bartholomäus Ziegenbalg**, began at **Tranquebar in 1706**. The **'Serampore Trio'** (William Carey, Joshua Marshman and William Ward) worked from the Danish enclave of **Serampore near Calcutta** from 1800. **Don't confuse** the Portuguese were the **first** Europeans to bring (Catholic) Christian missions to India, not the last.

**Remember it** First factories: Dutch = Masulipatnam, English = Surat, Danish = Tranquebar, French = Pondicherry.

**TL;DR**

- Dutch: first factory Masulipatnam (1605); Fort Geldria, Pulicat = Coromandel HQ; beaten by the English at Bedara (1759).
- English EIC chartered 1600; Surat (1612–13), Madras (1639), Bombay (1668); Roe's farman from Jahangir (1615).
- Danish company 1616; Tranquebar (1620); sold to the British 1845.
- French: Pondicherry founded 1674 (Francois Martin); Dupleix (governor from 1742) pioneered political interference.
keyPoints: Dutch: first factory Masulipatnam (1605); Fort Geldria at Pulicat = Coromandel HQ.
English EIC chartered 1600; Surat (1612–13), Madras/Fort St. George (1639), Bombay (dowry 1661, EIC 1668).
Sir Thomas Roe secured a trade farman from Jahangir in 1615.
Danish company 1616; Tranquebar (1620); sold to British in 1845.
French: Pondicherry founded by Francois Martin (1674); Dupleix pioneered political intervention.
Danish towns hosted the first Protestant mission (Ziegenbalg, Tranquebar, 1706) and the Serampore Trio (near Calcutta).

items.title: European Factories on the Andhra (Coromandel) Coast
items.body:
**In one line** The European trading posts (factories) strung along the Andhra 'Coromandel' coast, and which power first held each one.

**Why it is asked** This is the AP-specific angle APPSC prizes — matching a coastal town (Masulipatnam, Pulicat, Yanam) to the right European power, and remembering Yanam's later merger with India.

**The story**

The **Coromandel coast** of Andhra produced world-famous **painted and printed cotton cloth (Kalamkari)** and lay on the sea lane between Bengal and the south, so every company wanted a base here. The **Dutch** opened their very first Indian factory at **Masulipatnam (1605)**, the chief port of the Golconda kingdom, and made **Pulicat (Fort Geldria)** their Coromandel headquarters; they also held **Bheemunipatnam** near Visakhapatnam. The **English** set up early at **Masulipatnam (1611)** and **Nizampatnam (Pettapoli)** in the Krishna delta. The **French** also opened a factory at **Masulipatnam (1669)**, so the Dutch, English and French all traded from this one port. The French held **Yanam** near the mouth of the Godavari; the British captured it in the Carnatic wars, but the **Treaty of Paris (1763)**, which ended the Third Carnatic War, **restored Yanam to France**. Yanam stayed French even after India's independence in 1947 and only **merged with India in 1954**; today it is part of the **Union Territory of Puducherry**.

**Picture it**

| Town (modern name) | First / chief European power | Note |
|---|---|---|
| Masulipatnam (Machilipatnam) | Dutch (1605, first factory) | Chief Golconda port; English factory 1611 |
| Pulicat | Dutch — Fort Geldria | HQ of Dutch Coromandel |
| Nizampatnam (Pettapoli) | English | Southern Krishna delta |
| Bheemunipatnam (Bimlipatam) | Dutch | Near Visakhapatnam |
| Yanam (Yanaon) | French | Near the Godavari mouth; merged 1954 |

**Terms explained**

- **Coromandel coast** — the south-eastern coast of India (south of the Krishna river), covering coastal Andhra and Tamil Nadu.
- **Kalamkari** — hand-painted or block-printed cotton cloth; 'kalam' means pen.
- **Union Territory** — a region governed directly by the central government rather than by a state.

**Don't confuse** On the AP coast, **Masulipatnam and Pulicat were Dutch**, **Nizampatnam was English**, and **Yanam was French** — do not mix the three.

**Remember it** AP coast owners: **D**utch at Masulipatnam and Pulicat, **E**nglish at Nizampatnam, **F**rench at Yanam.

**TL;DR**

- Masulipatnam: Dutch first factory (1605); chief Golconda port; later an English factory (1611).
- Pulicat: Dutch Fort Geldria = Coromandel HQ.
- Nizampatnam = English; Bheemunipatnam = Dutch.
- Yanam = French enclave, merged with India in 1954 (now Puducherry UT).
keyPoints: Masulipatnam: Dutch first factory (1605), English factory (1611); chief Golconda port.
Pulicat: Dutch Fort Geldria — headquarters of Dutch Coromandel.
Nizampatnam (Pettapoli) hosted an early English factory; Bheemunipatnam was a Dutch settlement.
Yanam was a French enclave near the Godavari, merged with India in 1954 (now Puducherry UT).
The Andhra coast was prized for its painted cotton textiles.
Masulipatnam hosted Dutch (1605), English (1611) and French (1669) factories; Yanam was restored to France by the Treaty of Paris (1763).
items.mnemonic: AP coast: Masulipatnam & Pulicat = Dutch, Nizampatnam = English, Yanam = French.

items.title: The Carnatic Wars & the Northern Circars (1746–63)
items.body:
**In one line** The three Anglo-French wars fought in south India (1746–63) that decided which European power would dominate, and how the British won the Andhra 'Northern Circars'.

**Why it is asked** The treaty that ended each war, the Battle of Wandiwash, and the five Northern Circars tracts are standard match-and-sequence questions.

**The story**

As the Mughal empire weakened, the English and French both tried to fill the power vacuum in the south by **backing rival candidates** for the thrones of Hyderabad and the Carnatic. In the **First Carnatic War (1746–48)** the French captured Madras; it ended with the **Treaty of Aix-la-Chapelle (1748)**, which gave Madras back to the English. In the **Second War (1749–54)**, **Robert Clive's capture and 53-day defence of Arcot (1751)** broke French momentum; it ended with the **Treaty of Pondicherry** after France recalled **Dupleix**. In the **Third War (1756–63)**, **Sir Eyre Coote defeated the French under Count de Lally at the Battle of Wandiwash (1760)**; Pondicherry fell in 1761 and the **Treaty of Paris (1763)** ended French political ambitions. These wars proved that small, **European-trained armies** could beat much larger Indian forces.

Meanwhile the French general **Bussy** had obtained the **Northern Circars** (the five coastal Andhra tracts) as a grant from the Nizam of Hyderabad. During the Third War the **Nizam transferred Masulipatnam and the Circars to the British**, who confirmed the gift through a **Mughal farman (1765)** and a treaty with the Nizam (1766); the **Guntur Circar** passed fully to them in **1788**.

**Picture it**

| War | Years | Key event | Ended by |
|---|---|---|---|
| First | 1746–48 | French take Madras; Battle of San Thome | Treaty of Aix-la-Chapelle |
| Second | 1749–54 | Clive defends Arcot (1751); Dupleix recalled | Treaty of Pondicherry |
| Third | 1756–63 | Battle of Wandiwash (1760) — Coote beats Lally | Treaty of Paris (1763) |

**Terms explained**

- **Carnatic** — the region of the south-east coast around Arcot and Madras.
- **Northern Circars** — the five coastal Andhra tracts: **Srikakulam (Chicacole), Rajahmundry, Eluru, Kondapalli and Guntur**.
- **Farman** — a Mughal royal grant or permit.

**Don't confuse** The **First** war ended at **Aix-la-Chapelle**, the **Second** at **Pondicherry**, the **Third** at **Paris** — keep the three treaties in that order.

**Remember it** Carnatic War enders in order: **A**ix-la-Chapelle → (Treaty of) **P**ondicherry → **P**aris.

**TL;DR**

- First War (1746–48) → Treaty of Aix-la-Chapelle; Madras restored.
- Second War (1749–54) → Clive at Arcot; Treaty of Pondicherry; Dupleix recalled.
- Third War → Wandiwash (1760, Coote v. Lally); Treaty of Paris (1763).
- Northern Circars (5 tracts) went from Bussy/French to the British; farman 1765, Guntur 1788.
keyPoints: First Carnatic War (1746–48) ended with the Treaty of Aix-la-Chapelle; Madras restored.
Second Carnatic War (1749–54): Clive's Arcot exploit; Treaty of Pondicherry; Dupleix recalled.
Third Carnatic War: Battle of Wandiwash (1760, Eyre Coote v. Lally); Treaty of Paris (1763).
Northern Circars = Srikakulam, Rajahmundry, Eluru, Kondapalli, Guntur.
Bussy got the Circars from the Nizam; transferred to the British, confirmed by 1765 farman; Guntur in 1788.
items.mnemonic: Carnatic War enders 'ACP': Aix-la-Chapelle → (Treaty of) Pondicherry → Paris.

items.title: Plassey, Buxar & the Turn to Territorial Power
items.body:
**In one line** How two battles in Bengal — Plassey (1757) and Buxar (1764) — turned the English Company from a trader into the ruler of eastern India.

**Why it is asked** Who fought whom at each battle, and what the Treaty of Allahabad and the 'Diwani' meant, are among the most-asked modern-history facts.

**The story**

The Nawab of Bengal, **Siraj-ud-Daulah**, clashed with the Company over its misuse of trade privileges and the fortification of Calcutta (the 'Black Hole' episode). At the **Battle of Plassey (1757)**, **Robert Clive** won not by hard fighting but through the **treachery of Mir Jafar**, the Nawab's commander, who was then made puppet Nawab. Plassey gave the Company military control of Bengal and vast wealth. A later Nawab, **Mir Qasim**, tried to resist and allied with **Shuja-ud-Daulah of Awadh** and the Mughal emperor **Shah Alam II**. At the **Battle of Buxar (1764)**, **Hector Munro** defeated this three-way alliance — because it beat a Mughal-led coalition, Buxar was **more decisive than Plassey**. In the **Treaty of Allahabad (1765)**, Clive obtained from Shah Alam II the **Diwani** — the right to collect revenue — of **Bengal, Bihar and Orissa**. Collecting the land revenue of India's richest province turned the Company into a **territorial ruler**.

**Picture it**

| Battle / treaty | Year | Who | Result |
|---|---|---|---|
| Plassey | 1757 | Clive v. Siraj-ud-Daulah (Mir Jafar betrays) | British supremacy in Bengal |
| Buxar | 1764 | Munro v. Mir Qasim + Shuja-ud-Daulah + Shah Alam II | Company masters eastern India |
| Treaty of Allahabad | 1765 | Clive and Shah Alam II | Company gets the Diwani |

**Terms explained**

- **Nawab** — a Mughal provincial governor who became an independent ruler as the empire declined.
- **Diwani** — the right to collect the land **revenue** (taxes) of a province.
- **Buffer state** — a weak, friendly state (here Awadh) kept between the Company and its rivals.

**Don't confuse** **Plassey (1757)** was won by *betrayal* against *one* Nawab; **Buxar (1764)** was a *real battle* against a *three-power alliance* and gave the Company the Diwani.

**Remember it** Plassey = **Plot** (1757); Buxar = **Coalition** (1764); Allahabad = **Diwani** (1765).

**TL;DR**

- Plassey (1757): Clive beat Siraj-ud-Daulah through Mir Jafar's betrayal.
- Buxar (1764): Munro beat Mir Qasim + Shuja-ud-Daulah + Shah Alam II.
- Buxar was more decisive than Plassey for political mastery of the east.
- Treaty of Allahabad (1765) gave the Company the Diwani of Bengal, Bihar and Orissa — the trader became a ruler.
keyPoints: Plassey (1757): Clive beat Siraj-ud-Daulah via Mir Jafar's betrayal; British supremacy in Bengal.
Buxar (1764): Munro beat Mir Qasim + Shuja-ud-Daulah + Shah Alam II — a Mughal-led coalition.
Buxar was more decisive than Plassey for British political mastery of the east.
Treaty of Allahabad (1765) gave the Company the Diwani of Bengal, Bihar and Orissa.
The Company thus turned from trader to territorial ruler; Awadh kept as a buffer state.

items.title: Charter Acts, Early Factories, Trade Goods & Missions (PYQ set)
items.body:
**In one line** A cluster of exam-repeat facts — early English factories, Anglo-Dutch clashes, Bengal trade goods, the Charter Acts, and the first Christian missions.

**Why it is asked** Each of these has appeared in UPSC/APPSC prelims (Broach 2021, Bengal exports 2018, Charter Act 1813 in 2019, St Francis Xavier 2021), so they are high-probability one-markers.

**The story**

The earliest English factory came at **Surat (1613)** after the **Battle of Swally (Suvali, 1612)**, where the English beat the Portuguese fleet and won Jahangir's goodwill; **Broach (Bharuch)** was among the first inland factories. The **Amboyna Massacre (1623)** in the East Indies made the English give up the spice islands and concentrate on the Indian mainland, and the Dutch were finally beaten in India at the **Battle of Bedara (1759)**. From Bengal the Company exported **cotton textiles, raw silk, saltpetre and opium** — saltpetre (used to make gunpowder) and Bengal silk and muslin were especially prized. The Jesuit **St Francis Xavier**, who evangelised Portuguese India, lies entombed at the **Basilica of Bom Jesus, Old Goa** (he died on Shangchuan Island, China, in 1552). The Company's trading monopoly was then wound down in steps by the **Charter Acts**, and Company rule itself ended after the 1857 revolt.

**Picture it**

| Charter Act | Key provision |
|---|---|
| 1813 | Ended the EIC's trade monopoly **except tea and the China trade**; asserted Crown sovereignty; ₹1 lakh for education |
| 1833 | Ended **all** EIC trade; created the **Governor-General of India** (Bentinck first) |
| 1853 | Open competition for the Civil Service |

**Terms explained**

- **Monopoly** — the sole legal right to carry on a trade; the Charter Acts gradually removed the Company's monopoly.
- **Saltpetre** — potassium nitrate, the key ingredient of gunpowder.
- **Proclamation of 1858** — Queen Victoria's announcement placing India under the British Crown and ending Company rule.

**Don't confuse** The **Charter Act of 1813** only ended the monopoly (except tea/China); it was the **Charter Act of 1833** that ended *all* Company trade and created the Governor-General of India.

**Remember it** Charter Acts remove trade in steps: **1813** (except tea/China) → **1833** (all trade ends, GG of India) → **1853** (civil-service exam).

**TL;DR**

- Surat (1613) followed the Battle of Swally (1612); Broach was an early inland factory.
- Amboyna (1623) pushed the English to the mainland; the Dutch were beaten at Bedara (1759).
- Bengal staple exports: cotton textiles, raw silk, saltpetre, opium.
- Charter Acts 1813/1833/1853 ended Company trade; GoI Act 1858 and the Queen's Proclamation ended Company rule.
- St Francis Xavier (Jesuit) is entombed at the Bom Jesus Basilica, Old Goa; first Protestant mission at Tranquebar (1706, Ziegenbalg).
keyPoints: Surat factory (1613) followed the Battle of Swally (1612) vs the Portuguese; Broach was an early inland factory.
Amboyna Massacre (1623) pushed the English from the spice islands to mainland India; Dutch beaten at Bedara (1759).
Bengal staple exports (mid-18th c.): cotton textiles, raw silk, saltpetre and opium.
Charter Act 1813 ended EIC monopoly except tea & China trade; 1833 ended all trade + created GG of India; 1853 opened Civil Service.
Company rule ended by GoI Act 1858 + Queen Victoria's Proclamation (1 Nov 1858).
St Francis Xavier (Jesuit) is entombed at Bom Jesus Basilica, Old Goa; died on Shangchuan I., China (1552).
items.mnemonic: Charter Acts end trade in steps: 1813 (except tea/China) → 1833 (all trade ends, GG of India) → 1853 (civil-service exam).

items.title: Portuguese India — full chronology, policies and decline
items.body:
### Portuguese India — full chronology, policies and decline

**In one line**
From Diaz (1487) to Operation Vijay (1961): every Portuguese date, place and policy that exams ask.

**The story**
**Diaz** reached the **Cape of Storms** in 1487; **Vasco da Gama** came to Calicut in 1498 with **three ships**, piloted by **Abdul Majid**. **Cabral** followed in **1500**. Forts rose at Cochin (1503) and **Cannanore** (1505). **Almeida**, the **first viceroy**, lost at **Chaul** (1508) but won at Diu (1509), and enforced the **cartaz** (sea **pass**). **Albuquerque** took Goa (1510) from **Yusuf Adil Shah**, banned **sati**, encouraged **Indian wives**, and the Portuguese spread **tobacco** and **cashew**. Under Nino da Cunha came **Bassein** (1534) and **Diu**; Bahadur Shah died in 1537. **Daman** fell in **1559**. Goa got the first **printing press** (**1556**) and the **Inquisition** (**1560**). **Hugli** was lost to Shah Jahan in **1632**; the **Malabar** forts went to the Dutch by **1663**. **Dadra** came in **1779**, **Panjim** became capital in **1843**, and **Operation Vijay** ended it all in 1961. **Jesuits**, intolerance and **piracy** explain the decline.

#### Portuguese timeline

| Year | Event |
|---|---|
| **1487** | **Bartholomeu Diaz** reached the tip of Africa, named it the **Cape of Storms**; renamed Cape of Good Hope |
| **1498** | Da Gama came with **three ships**; a Gujarati pilot, **Abdul Majid**, guided him from Malindi to Calicut |
| **1500** | **Pedro Alvares Cabral** led the second voyage and set up a factory at Calicut |
| **1502** | Da Gama’s second voyage — bombarded Calicut and burnt its fleet |
| **1505** | Second fort at **Cannanore** (Kannur); Almeida arrives as first viceroy |
| **1505–09** | **Almeida**, the **first viceroy**, followed the Blue Water Policy |
| **1508** | **Battle of Chaul** — Egyptian (Mamluk) and Gujarati fleet beat the Portuguese; Almeida’s son Lourenço killed |
| **Cartaz** | A Portuguese sea **pass** every Asian ship had to buy; ships without one were seized |
| **1510** | Albuquerque captured Goa from **Yusuf Adil Shah** of Bijapur |
| **Albuquerque** | Banned **sati** in Goa; encouraged Portuguese men to take **Indian wives** |
| **New crops** | Portuguese brought **tobacco**, **cashew**, potato, chilli and new coconut varieties |
| **1534** | **Treaty of Bassein** — Bahadur Shah of Gujarat ceded Bassein (the PDF says he captured it) |
| **1535–37** | Fort at **Diu** (1535); Bahadur Shah drowned near the Portuguese ships (**1537**); Siege of Diu repelled (1538–39) |
| **1559** | **Daman** taken |
| **1556** | First **printing press** in India, at St Paul’s College, Goa |
| **1560** | Goa **Inquisition** — religious persecution that turned Indians against the Portuguese |
| **1579 / 1632** | **Hugli** settled under Akbar’s farman; taken by Shah Jahan’s general Qasim Khan in **1632** over slaving and piracy |
| **East coast** | **San Thome** (Mylapore) and **Chittagong** — Portuguese posts outside the west coast |
| **1663** | Lost all **Malabar** forts (Cochin, Cannanore) to the Dutch |
| **1779** | Acquired **Dadra** and Nagar Haveli (from the Marathas); freed by local volunteers in 1954 |
| **1843** | **Panjim** (Nova Goa) replaced Old Goa as capital |
| **Dec 1961** | **Operation Vijay** ended 451 years of Portuguese rule in Goa, Daman and Diu |
| **Decline** | Intolerance (**Jesuits**, Inquisition), **piracy** and slaving that angered the Mughals, small home country, Dutch and English rivals |

**Don't confuse**
- **Chaul (1508)** was a Portuguese *defeat*; **Diu (1509)** their *victory*.
- **Almeida** = first viceroy, Blue Water, cartaz; **Albuquerque** = Goa, sati ban.
- **Hugli** was lost to **Shah Jahan** (1632), not Aurangzeb.

**TL;DR**
- Diaz 1487, da Gama 1498, Cabral 1500; Cochin 1503, Cannanore 1505.
- Almeida: first viceroy, cartaz; Chaul 1508 lost, Diu 1509 won.
- Albuquerque Goa 1510 (Bijapur); Bassein 1534, Diu 1535, Daman 1559; press 1556.
- Hugli lost 1632; Malabar lost 1663; Dadra 1779; Panjim 1843; Operation Vijay 1961.
keyPoints: Diaz reached the Cape of Storms (1487); da Gama came with three ships (1498); Cabral led the second voyage (1500).
Almeida was the first viceroy; the cartaz was a compulsory Portuguese sea pass.
Albuquerque banned sati in Goa; the Portuguese introduced tobacco and cashew.
The first printing press in India was set up at Goa in 1556.
Shah Jahan captured Hugli (1632); Operation Vijay liberated Goa (1961).

items.title: The Dutch and the Danes — settlements, battles and exit
items.body:
### The Dutch and the Danes — settlements, battles and exit

**In one line**
The Dutch held the Coromandel and spice trade till the English beat them; the Danes were small traders but big missionaries.

**The story**
The **VOC** (**1602**) opened Masulipatnam (1605), then **Pulicat** (**1610**, Fort Geldria) and Surat (1616). On the Andhra coast it also had **Palakollu**, **Draksharama** and Bheemunipatnam. In Bengal it held **Chinsura** (**Fort Gustavus**); **Nagapattinam** became HQ in **1690**, and **Cochin** fell to it in 1663. The **Amboyna** Massacre (**1623**) drove the English out of the spice islands. But **Marthanda Varma** beat the Dutch at **Colachel** (1741) and the English crushed them at **Bedara** (**1759**). The treaty of **1824** ended Dutch India. Their trade was **redistributive**. The Danes (**1616**, **Christian IV**) took Tranquebar from **Thanjavur** and built **Fort Dansborg**; **Serampore** (**Frederiksnagore**) was their Bengal town. They were known for **missionary** work, and **sold** out in **1845**.

#### Dutch settlements and battles

| Year | Event | Region |
|---|---|---|
| **1602** | **VOC** (Vereenigde Oost-Indische Compagnie) formed | — |
| **1610** | Pulicat — **Fort Geldria**; HQ of Dutch Coromandel until 1690 | AP/TN border |
| **1616** | Surat factory | Gujarat |
| **17th c.** | **Palakollu**, **Draksharama**, Jagannathapuram (Kakinada) and Bheemunipatnam (Bimlipatam) | Godavari delta, AP |
| **1653** | **Chinsura** — **Fort Gustavus**; also Kasimbazar, Patna, Balasore | Bengal |
| **1659 / 1690** | **Nagapattinam** taken from the Portuguese; HQ moved there from Pulicat in **1690** | Tamil Nadu |
| **1663** | Took **Cochin** from the Portuguese | Kerala |
| **1623** | **Amboyna** Massacre — English withdrew from Indonesia to India | Moluccas |
| **1741** | **Colachel** — **Marthanda Varma** of Travancore beat the Dutch; De Lannoy joined Travancore | Kerala |
| **1759** | **Bedara** (near Chinsura) — English (Forde) beat the Dutch; end of Dutch ambitions in India | Bengal |
| **1824** | Anglo-Dutch Treaty — India to Britain, Indonesia to the Dutch | — |
| **Policy** | **Redistributive** (carrying) trade: Coromandel cloth exchanged for spices | Asia |

#### The Danes

| Year | Fact |
|---|---|
| **1616** | Company chartered by King **Christian IV** |
| **1620** | Tranquebar (Tharangambadi) granted by the Nayak of **Thanjavur**; **Fort Dansborg** (the PDF gives 1628) |
| **1755** | **Serampore** (**Frederiksnagore**) on the Hooghly — main Danish town |
| **Character** | Better known for **missionary** work (Ziegenbalg, Serampore Trio) than commerce |
| **1845** | **Sold** all settlements to the British (the PDF table says 1745) |

**Don't confuse**
- **Colachel (1741)** = Dutch lost to **Travancore**; **Bedara (1759)** = Dutch lost to the **English**.
- Dutch Coromandel HQ: **Pulicat** until 1690, then **Nagapattinam**.
- Danish dates: **1616** company, **1620** Tranquebar, **1845** sold.

**TL;DR**
- VOC 1602; Pulicat 1610; Surat 1616; Chinsura 1653; Nagapattinam HQ 1690.
- Amboyna 1623; Colachel 1741; Bedara 1759; exit 1824.
- Danes: 1616, Tranquebar/Fort Dansborg 1620, Serampore 1755, sold 1845.
keyPoints: VOC formed 1602; Fort Geldria at Pulicat (1610) was the Coromandel HQ till Nagapattinam (1690).
Dutch factories in AP: Masulipatnam, Palakollu, Draksharama, Bheemunipatnam.
Marthanda Varma beat the Dutch at Colachel (1741); the English beat them at Bedara (1759).
Danish Fort Dansborg at Tranquebar; Serampore (Frederiksnagore); sold 1845.

items.title: The English Company — from charter to Calcutta (1600–1717)
items.body:
### The English Company — from charter to Calcutta (1600–1717)

**In one line**
Every early English step: charter, voyages, envoys, factories, the three Presidency towns and the farmans that made the Company rich.

**The story**
The charter gave the **Merchants of London** a **15**-year monopoly. **Lancaster**'s first voyage went to Java. **Hawkins** (ship **Hector**) failed at Jahangir’s court, but **Masulipatnam** got a factory in **1611**, and **Thomas Best**'s win at **Swally** opened Surat. **Roe**, envoy of **James I**, came in **1615**. On the south coast came **Armagaon** (**1626**) and the Golconda **Golden Farman** (**500 pagodas**, 1632); in Orissa **Hariharpur** (**1633**). **Francis Day** leased Madras from **Venkatadri** (1639). **Shah Shuja** allowed Hugli for **Rs 3,000**. Bombay came for **£10** in **1668**; **Aungier** built it and the HQ moved there in **1687**. **Child's War** against **Aurangzeb** failed. **Job Charnock** settled **Sutanati** (1690); **Kalikata** and **Gobindapur** were added in 1698, and Fort William got **Charles Eyre** (**1700**). Rivals merged into the **United Company** (**1708**). **Farrukhsiyar**’s farman (1717), the **Magna Carta**, gave the **dastak**. **Visakhapatnam** had a factory from **1682**.

#### English milestones

| Year | Event |
|---|---|
| **31 Dec 1600** | Elizabeth I chartered “The Governor and Company of **Merchants of London** Trading into the East Indies” — **15**-year monopoly east of the Cape |
| **1601** | First voyage under **James Lancaster** — Sumatra and Java, not India |
| **1608–11** | Captain **William Hawkins** (ship **Hector**) at Jahangir’s court — title “English Khan”; the Portuguese blocked him |
| **1611** | **Masulipatnam** — first English factory on the east coast (ship Globe); also Petapoli (Nizampatnam) |
| **1612** | Captain **Thomas Best** defeated the Portuguese at **Swally** — Jahangir allowed the Surat factory (1613) |
| **1615–19** | Sir Thomas Roe, envoy of **James I**, won a farman to trade and set up factories (Agra, Ahmedabad, Broach) |
| **1626** | **Armagaon** (Durgarajupatnam, near Pulicat) — first fortified English post in the south |
| **1632** | **Golden Farman** of the Golconda Sultan — free trade in Golconda ports for **500 pagodas** a year |
| **1633** | **Hariharpur** and Balasore (Orissa) — first English factories in the east |
| **1639** | **Francis Day** leased Madras from Damarla **Venkatadri** Nayaka (Chandragiri/Vijayanagara); Fort St George; east-coast HQ from 1641 |
| **1651** | Hugli factory — Bengal governor **Shah Shuja** allowed trade for **Rs 3,000** a year |
| **1668** | Charles II gave Bombay (his 1661 dowry) to the Company for **£10** a year |
| **1669–77 / 1687** | **Gerald Aungier** — founder of Bombay; western HQ moved from Surat in **1687** |
| **1686–90** | **Child's War** — the Company under Josiah Child fought **Aurangzeb**, lost, was fined Rs 1.5 lakh |
| **1690** | **Job Charnock** at **Sutanati** — start of Calcutta |
| **1698** | Zamindari of Sutanati, **Kalikata** and **Gobindapur** (from Azim-us-Shan) — the three villages became Calcutta |
| **1700** | Fort William — Bengal Presidency; first President **Charles Eyre** |
| **1698–1708** | Rival “English Company” merged with the old one — **United Company** of Merchants (**1708**) |
| **1717** | **Farrukhsiyar**’s farman (John Surman mission) — the Company's **Magna Carta**; dastaks for duty-free trade |
| **Dastak** | Free pass for duty-free goods; misused for servants’ private trade |
| **1682** | **Visakhapatnam** factory (north Andhra coast) |

**Don't confuse**
- **Hawkins** (1608) failed; **Roe** (1615) succeeded — both at **Jahangir**'s court.
- First English factory overall = **Surat (1613)**; first on the **east coast** = **Masulipatnam (1611)**.
- **Golden Farman (1632)** = Golconda; **Farrukhsiyar's farman (1717)** = Mughal 'Magna Carta'.

**TL;DR**
- Charter 31 Dec 1600; Lancaster 1601; Hawkins 1608; Masulipatnam 1611; Swally 1612; Roe 1615.
- Armagaon 1626; Golden Farman 1632; Hariharpur 1633; Madras 1639; Hugli 1651; Bombay 1668.
- Child's War 1686–90; Sutanati 1690; three villages 1698; Fort William 1700; United Company 1708; Farrukhsiyar 1717.
keyPoints: Hawkins came on the Hector (1608); Thomas Best won at Swally (1612); Roe was James I's envoy (1615).
Masulipatnam (1611) was the first English factory on the east coast; Armagaon (1626) near Pulicat.
Golden Farman (1632): Golconda trade for 500 pagodas a year; Francis Day leased Madras from Damarla Venkatadri (1639).
Bombay leased for £10 (1668); Gerald Aungier founder of Bombay; Job Charnock founded Sutanati (1690).
Farrukhsiyar's farman (1717) — the Company's Magna Carta — gave dastaks.

items.title: The French — company, settlements, governors and exit
items.body:
### The French — company, settlements, governors and exit

**In one line**
The French came last (1664), built a chain of five towns and nearly won the south under Dupleix before losing to the English.

**The story**
**Colbert** set up the company under **Louis XIV** in 1664. **Caron** opened Surat (**1668**), and Golconda granted **Masulipatnam** (**1669**). **Sher Khan Lodi** of **Valikondapuram** gave Martin the Pondicherry site. **Shaista Khan** granted **Chandernagore**. The Dutch held Pondicherry until **Ryswick** (1697). **Mahe**, Yanam and **Karaikal** followed. After **Dumas**, **Dupleix** (**1742**) trained Indian **sepoys** and meddled in succession wars. After the Carnatic defeats **Lally** was executed (**1766**). Chandernagore joined India in **1950**; the rest followed on **1 November 1954**, and de jure in **1962**.

#### French settlements and people

| Year | Fact |
|---|---|
| **1664** | **Colbert**, minister of **Louis XIV** — a state-controlled company (last to come) |
| **1668** | **Francois Caron** — first French factory at Surat |
| **1669** | Factory at **Masulipatnam** by a Golconda grant |
| **1673–74** | **Sher Khan Lodi** (**Valikondapuram**, Bijapur) granted Pondicherry; Martin founded it 1674 |
| **1690** | **Chandernagore** — granted by **Shaista Khan**, governor of Bengal |
| **1693–97** | Dutch held Pondicherry; returned by the Treaty of **Ryswick** |
| **1725–39** | **Mahe** 1725, Yanam 1731, **Karaikal** 1739 — with Pondicherry the later five French towns |
| **1720s–41** | Governors Lenoir and **Dumas** revived the company before Dupleix |
| **1742–54** | **Dupleix** governor; formed mixed Indian–French regiments (the PDF gives 1741) |
| **Sepoys** | French first trained Indians as **sepoys** in European drill |
| **1766** | **Lally** beheaded in Paris for the defeat |
| **1950 / 1954** | Chandernagore — de facto to India **1950** (after a 1949 plebiscite); merged with West Bengal 1954 |
| **1954 / 1962** | De facto transfer **1 November 1954**; Treaty of Cession (1956) ratified **1962**; UT of Puducherry |

**Don't confuse**
- **First** French factory = **Surat (1668)**; **chief** settlement = **Pondicherry (1674)**.
- **Shaista Khan** granted Chandernagore; **Sher Khan Lodi** granted Pondicherry.
- **1954** = de facto transfer; **1962** = de jure.

**TL;DR**
- Colbert 1664 (Louis XIV); Caron Surat 1668; Masulipatnam 1669; Pondicherry 1674 (Sher Khan Lodi).
- Chandernagore 1690 (Shaista Khan); Ryswick 1697; Mahe 1725, Yanam 1731, Karaikal 1739.
- Dupleix 1742; Lally executed 1766; Chandernagore 1950; others 1 Nov 1954 (de jure 1962).
keyPoints: Colbert founded the French company under Louis XIV (1664); Francois Caron opened Surat (1668).
Sher Khan Lodi, governor of Valikondapuram, granted Pondicherry; Shaista Khan granted Chandernagore.
The French were first to train Indian sepoys; Dupleix became governor in 1742.
French towns: de facto transfer 1 November 1954, de jure 1962.

items.title: Carnatic Wars — every battle, person and treaty term
items.body:
### Carnatic Wars — every battle, person and treaty term

**In one line**
The people, battles and terms of the three Anglo-French wars, war by war.

**The story**
The First War grew from the **Austrian Succession**: **La Bourdonnais** of **Mauritius** took Madras, a tiny French force beat **Mahfuz Khan** on the **Adyar**, and Madras was traded back for **Louisbourg**. In the Second, **Anwaruddin** died at **Ambur**. The English backed **Muhammad Ali** and **Nasir Jung**, and **Bussy** installed **Salabat Jung**. Clive’s **53-day** defence of Arcot saved **Trichinopoly**, and **Chanda Sahib** was **executed**. **Godeheu** made peace — both sides agreed **not to interfere**. The Third was part of the **Seven Years** War: Clive and **Watson** took **Chandernagore**, Lally took **Fort St David** (**Cuddalore**), Wandiwash was fought on **22 January 1760**, and Pondicherry and **Mahe** fell in **1761**. Paris gave the towns back but forbade any **fortif**ication. **Naval** power and **Bengal** money decided it.

#### The three wars

| War | When | Event |
|---|---|---|
| First | Background | Extension of the War of the **Austrian Succession** |
| First | Sept 1746 | **La Bourdonnais** (governor of **Mauritius**) took Madras |
| First | 1746 | Battle of St Thome/**Adyar** — French (Paradis) beat **Mahfuz Khan**, son of Nawab Anwaruddin |
| First | 1748 | Madras swapped for **Louisbourg** (North America) |
| Second | 1749 | **Ambur** — Nawab **Anwaruddin** killed |
| Second | 1749–54 | French: Chanda Sahib + Muzaffar Jung; English: **Muhammad Ali** + **Nasir Jung** |
| Second | 1751 | **Bussy** made **Salabat Jung** Nizam |
| Second | 1751 | Clive at Arcot — **53-day** siege, diverting French from **Trichinopoly** |
| Second | 1752 | **Chanda Sahib** beaten (Kaveripakkam) and **executed** |
| Second | 1754–55 | **Godeheu** replaced Dupleix and signed the Treaty of Pondicherry (dated 1754 or 1755) |
| Second | Terms | Both companies agreed **not to interfere** in princes’ affairs |
| Third | Background | Part of the **Seven Years**’ War |
| Third | Mar 1757 | Clive and Admiral **Watson** took **Chandernagore** |
| Third | 1758 | Lally took **Fort St David** (**Cuddalore**); Madras siege lifted by Pocock’s fleet |
| Third | 22 Jan 1760 | Wandiwash (Vandavasi) — Coote beat Lally; Bussy captured |
| Third | 1761 | Pondicherry fell (16 Jan **1761**); **Mahe** also lost |
| Third | 1763 | Towns returned, but France could not **fortif**y them or keep troops |
| Result | Why | **Naval** supremacy, **Bengal** revenue, private-company backing; French company was state-run |

**Don't confuse**
- **Madras ↔ Louisbourg** (1748), not Pondicherry.
- **Ambur (1749)** killed Anwaruddin; **Adyar (1746)** humbled his son Mahfuz Khan.
- **Godeheu**, not Dupleix, signed the Treaty of Pondicherry.

**TL;DR**
- First: Austrian Succession; La Bourdonnais; Adyar; Louisbourg swap.
- Second: Ambur 1749; Salabat Jung; Arcot 53 days; Godeheu.
- Third: Seven Years’ War; Wandiwash 22 Jan 1760; Pondicherry 1761; Paris 1763.
keyPoints: First Carnatic War = War of the Austrian Succession; La Bourdonnais took Madras; St Thome/Adyar (1746).
Madras was returned in exchange for Louisbourg (1748).
Anwaruddin was killed at Ambur (1749); Bussy made Salabat Jung Nizam; Godeheu replaced Dupleix.
Third war = Seven Years' War; Pondicherry fell 1761; English won through naval supremacy and Bengal's wealth.

items.title: Bengal 1717–1772 — Nawabs, conspirators, treaties and the Dual Government
items.body:
### Bengal 1717–1772 — Nawabs, conspirators, treaties and the Dual Government

**In one line**
The people and terms behind Plassey, Buxar and the Diwani — from Murshid Quli Khan to the end of the Dual Government.

**The story**
**Murshid Quli** Khan ruled from **Murshidabad**; **Alivardi** held the Europeans in check. Siraj renamed Calcutta **Alinagar**; **Holwell** said **123** died in the Black Hole. At Plassey (on the **Bhagirathi**, under **Alamgir II**), **Jagat Seth**, **Omichand** and Mir Jafar plotted, while **Mir Madan** and **Mohan Lal** stayed loyal. **Miran** had Siraj killed, and the Company got the **24 Parganas**. Mir Qasim ceded **Burdwan** and **Midnapore**, moved to **Monghyr**, and fought; Buxar came on **22 October 1764**. At Allahabad, Shah Alam got **Rs 26 lakh** and **Kara**, and Shuja paid **Rs 50 lakh**. The **Dual Government** left the Nawab only the **nizamat**, with **Reza Khan** and **Shitab Rai** as deputies. The **famine** of **1770** followed, and Hastings ended the system in **1772**.

#### People and terms

| Year | Fact |
|---|---|
| **1717–27** | **Murshid Quli** Khan — capital **Murshidabad** |
| **1740–56** | **Alivardi** Khan — compared Europeans to bees; resisted Maratha raids |
| **June 1756** | **Holwell**’s account: 146 confined, **123** died |
| **1756–57** | Calcutta renamed **Alinagar**; treaty of Feb 1757 |
| **1757** | Mir Jafar, Rai Durlabh, **Jagat Seth** (banker), **Omichand**, Manikchand |
| **23 June 1757** | **Mir Madan** and **Mohan Lal** fought for Siraj |
| **1757** | Palashi on the **Bhagirathi**; emperor **Alamgir II** |
| **1757** | Siraj murdered by **Miran**’s men |
| **1757** | Zamindari of the **24 Parganas** + huge cash |
| **1760** | Mir Qasim ceded **Burdwan**, **Midnapore**, Chittagong (the PDF credits Mir Jafar) |
| **1762–63** | Capital to **Monghyr**; abolished all internal duties |
| **22 Oct 1764** | Buxar (Bihar) — Munro won |
| **Aug 1765** | Shah Alam got **Rs 26 lakh** a year + **Kara** and Allahabad |
| **1765** | Shuja paid **Rs 50 lakh**; Awadh returned as buffer; Benares to Balwant Singh |
| **1765–72** | **Dual Government** — Company diwani, Nawab **nizamat** |
| **1765** | **Reza Khan** (Bengal), **Shitab Rai** (Bihar) |
| **1772** | Hastings ended it; Company took direct control |
| **1770** | Bengal **famine** — about a third died |

**Don't confuse**
- Company **paid** Shah Alam **Rs 26 lakh**; the PDF's '53 lakh' was the Nawab's nizamat allowance, not a payment by Shah Alam.
- **Diwani** = revenue (Company); **nizamat** = police and justice (Nawab).

**TL;DR**
- Murshid Quli → Alivardi → Siraj; Black Hole (Holwell, 123).
- Plassey: Jagat Seth, Omichand; loyal Mir Madan, Mohan Lal; 24 Parganas.
- Mir Qasim: Burdwan/Midnapore, Monghyr; Buxar 22 Oct 1764; Allahabad Rs 26 lakh; Dual Govt 1765–72.
keyPoints: Murshid Quli Khan moved the capital to Murshidabad; Alivardi Khan was Siraj’s grandfather.
Holwell’s Black Hole account claimed 123 deaths; Jagat Seth and Omichand joined the Plassey plot.
Mir Madan and Mohan Lal were loyal to Siraj; the 24 Parganas zamindari went to the Company.
Mir Qasim ceded Burdwan, Midnapore, Chittagong and shifted to Monghyr.
Shah Alam got Rs 26 lakh a year and Kara; Dual Government (1765–72) ended by Hastings in 1772.

items.title: Andhra under the Company — Northern Circars and the Ceded Districts
items.body:
### Andhra under the Company — Northern Circars and the Ceded Districts

**In one line**
How coastal Andhra (Circars) and Rayalaseema (Ceded Districts) passed from the Nizam to the British, step by step.

**The story**
**Bussy** got the Circars in **1753**. **Forde** beat the French at **Condore** and stormed Masulipatnam in **April 1759**; **Salabat Jung** **ceded** the port. The 1765 farman and the **1766** treaty followed, with the Company paying **tribute**. **Basalat Jung** held Guntur until 1782. In **1800** the Nizam gave up the **Ceded Districts**, where **Thomas Munro** was **Principal Collector**.

#### Coastal Andhra and Rayalaseema

| Year | Event |
|---|---|
| **1753** | Bussy got the Circars from Salabat Jung |
| **Dec 1758** | **Forde** beat Conflans at **Condore** (Chandurthi) |
| **April 1759** | Forde stormed Masulipatnam (Rajahmundry lost 1758) |
| **1759** | **Salabat Jung** **ceded** Masulipatnam to the English |
| **12 Nov 1766** | Treaty of Hyderabad with Nizam Ali — Company pays **tribute** (Rs 9 lakh a year) and supplies troops |
| **1782–88** | **Basalat Jung** held Guntur; British took it 1788 |
| **1800** | **Ceded Districts** (Cuddapah, Bellary, Kurnool, Anantapur area) for subsidiary troops |
| **1800–07** | **Thomas Munro** — **Principal Collector**; began ryotwari there |

**Don't confuse**
- **Northern Circars** = coastal Andhra (1759–88); **Ceded Districts** = Rayalaseema (1800).

**TL;DR**
- Bussy 1753; Condore 1758; Masulipatnam 1759; farman 1765; treaty 1766; Guntur 1788.
- Ceded Districts 1800; Thomas Munro Principal Collector.
keyPoints: Bussy got the Northern Circars in 1753; Forde won at Condore (1758) and took Masulipatnam (April 1759).
Basalat Jung held Guntur till 1782; it passed to the British in 1788.
The Nizam ceded the Ceded Districts (Rayalaseema) in 1800; Thomas Munro was their first Principal Collector.

items.title: Struggle for supremacy — Anglo-Mysore and Anglo-Maratha Wars
items.body:
### Struggle for supremacy — Anglo-Mysore and Anglo-Maratha Wars

**In one line**
After the French, the Company fought Mysore four times and the Marathas three times; each war ended with a treaty you must pair.

**The story**
**Hyder Ali** of **Dindigul** fought the First War, ended by the **Treaty of Madras** (**1769**). In the Second, Coote won at **Porto Novo**, Hyder died (**1782**), and **Mangalore** (**1784**) restored the status quo. Tipu's attack on **Travancore** brought **Cornwallis**: Seringapatam (1792) cost **half** the kingdom, including **Baramahal**. The Fourth War ended on **4 May 1799**; **Wodeyar** **Krishnaraja III** returned. Tipu had planted a **Tree of Liberty** and joined the **Jacobin** Club. With the Marathas, the **Treaty of Surat** (**Salsette**) was annulled at **Purandar** (**1776**). The English surrendered at **Wadgaon** (**1779**), and **Salbai** (**Mahadji**) ended the war. The **Barbhai** of **Nana Phadnavis** ruled Pune. **Baji Rao II** signed **Bassein**; Wellesley won at **Assaye**; **Deogaon** (**Cuttack**), **Surji** (**Scindia**) and **Rajpurghat** (**Holkar**) followed. The **Pindari** campaign led to **Sitabuldi** and **Mahidpur**, **Mandasor**, and exile at **Bithur**.

#### Anglo-Mysore Wars

| War | Who | Event / treaty |
|---|---|---|
| Hyder Ali | 1755 | Faujdar of **Dindigul**; French-trained arsenal |
| 1st (1767–69) | Hyder v. English (Gen. Smith) | **Treaty of Madras** (**1769**) — conquests returned, mutual help |
| 2nd (1780–84) | Coote beat Hyder | **Porto Novo** (1781); Hyder died **1782**; Tipu carried on |
| 2nd (1780–84) | Tipu v. English | **Treaty of Mangalore** (**1784**) — status quo |
| 3rd (1790–92) | Cause | Tipu attacked **Travancore**; **Cornwallis** led the war |
| 3rd (1790–92) | 1792 | Treaty of Seringapatam — **half** the kingdom (Malabar, Coorg, Dindigul, **Baramahal**) + Rs 3 crore; two sons as hostages |
| 4th (1799) | Wellesley | Tipu killed at Seringapatam, **4 May 1799**; no treaty |
| After 1799 | Settlement | **Wodeyar** **Krishnaraja III** restored; Nizam and British shared the rest |
| Tipu | Ideas | Planted a **Tree of Liberty**; member of the **Jacobin** Club; envoys to France and Turkey |

#### Anglo-Maratha Wars

| War | Year | Event / treaty |
|---|---|---|
| 1st (1775–82) | 1775 | **Treaty of Surat** — Raghoba gave **Salsette** and Bassein |
| 1st | 1774 | **Barbhai** (twelve) led by **Nana Phadnavis** for Sawai Madhavrao |
| 1st | 1776 | **Purandar** annulled Surat |
| 1st | 1779 | **Wadgaon** — English surrendered |
| 1st | 1782 | **Salbai** — via **Mahadji** Scindia; Salsette kept; Raghoba pensioned |
| 2nd (1803–05) | 1802 | **Treaty of Bassein** — **Baji Rao II** took subsidiary troops |
| 2nd | 1803 | Arthur Wellesley at **Assaye**; Lake at Delhi and Laswari |
| 2nd | 1803 | **Deogaon** — Bhonsle gave **Cuttack**, Balasore |
| 2nd | 1803 | **Surji**-Arjangaon — **Scindia** gave the doab, Delhi, Agra |
| 2nd | 1805 | **Rajpurghat** — **Holkar** gave up Tonk, Bundi |
| 3rd (1817–18) | Cause | Campaign against the **Pindari**s |
| 3rd | 1817–18 | Khadki, Koregaon (Peshwa), **Sitabuldi** (Bhonsle), **Mahidpur** (Holkar) |
| 3rd | 1818 | Peshwa pensioned at **Bithur**; Satara kept for Shivaji’s heir |
| 3rd | 1817–18 | Gwalior (Scindia) and **Mandasor** (Holkar) |

**Don't confuse**
- Mysore treaties: **Madras (1769) → Mangalore (1784) → Seringapatam (1792)**; 1799 had no treaty.
- Maratha: **Surat → Purandar → Wadgaon → Salbai** (1st); **Bassein, Deogaon, Surji-Arjangaon, Rajpurghat** (2nd).
- **Treaty of Bassein 1534** (Portuguese) ≠ **Treaty of Bassein 1802** (Peshwa).

**TL;DR**
- Mysore: Madras 1769, Mangalore 1784, Seringapatam 1792, fall 4 May 1799.
- Maratha I: Surat 1775, Purandar 1776, Wadgaon 1779, Salbai 1782.
- Maratha II: Bassein 1802, Deogaon, Surji-Arjangaon 1803, Rajpurghat 1805; III: Pindaris, Sitabuldi, Mahidpur, Bithur.
keyPoints: Treaty of Madras (1769) ended the 1st Anglo-Mysore War; Mangalore (1784) the 2nd.
Tipu ceded half his kingdom by the Treaty of Seringapatam (1792); died 4 May 1799.
Treaty of Salbai (1782) ended the 1st Anglo-Maratha War; Wadgaon (1779) was an English surrender.
Treaty of Bassein (1802): Baji Rao II accepted subsidiary alliance.
Third Anglo-Maratha War grew from the Pindari campaign; Peshwa exiled to Bithur.
Treaty of Surat (1775) was signed between Raghunathrao and Bombay (the Bombay government of the Company); the Treaty of Purandar (1776) annulled it.

items.title: Struggle for supremacy — Anglo-Sikh Wars and the annexation of Punjab
items.body:
### Struggle for supremacy — Anglo-Sikh Wars and the annexation of Punjab

**In one line**
Punjab was the last major independent kingdom; two wars (1845–49) made it British.

**The story**
Ranjit Singh accepted the **Sutlej** line at **Amritsar** (1809). After his death the First War brought **Mudki** to **Sobraon**, and the Treaty of **Lahore** gave Kashmir to **Gulab Singh**. **Bhairowal** put **Henry Lawrence** in charge. **Mulraj**'s revolt at **Multan** began the Second War — **Chillianwala**, then **Gujrat** — and Punjab was annexed on **29 March 1849**, with **Duleep Singh** pensioned.

#### Anglo-Sikh Wars

| Year | Event |
|---|---|
| 1809 | Treaty of **Amritsar** — Metcalfe; **Sutlej** frontier |
| 1845–46 | **Mudki**, Ferozeshah, Aliwal, **Sobraon** (decisive, 10 Feb 1846) |
| 1846 | Treaty of **Lahore**; Jullundur doab lost; Kashmir sold to **Gulab Singh** |
| 1846 | **Bhairowal** — Resident **Henry Lawrence** ran the regency |
| 1848 | Revolt of Diwan **Mulraj** at **Multan** |
| 1848–49 | Ramnagar, **Chillianwala**, **Gujrat** (decisive) |
| 1849 | Punjab annexed **29 March 1849**; **Duleep Singh** pensioned |

**Don't confuse**
- **Treaty of Amritsar 1809** (Ranjit Singh–Metcalfe) ≠ **Treaty of Amritsar 1846** (Kashmir to Gulab Singh).
- **Sobraon** ended the 1st war; **Gujrat** ended the 2nd.

**TL;DR**
- Amritsar 1809; 1st War — Mudki to Sobraon; Lahore and Bhairowal 1846.
- 2nd War — Mulraj, Chillianwala, Gujrat; annexation 29 March 1849.
keyPoints: Treaty of Amritsar (1809) fixed the Sutlej frontier.
Treaty of Lahore (1846) ended the 1st Anglo-Sikh War; Bhairowal set up Henry Lawrence as Resident.
Diwan Mulraj’s revolt at Multan began the 2nd War; Gujrat (1849) was decisive; Punjab annexed by Dalhousie.

items.title: For Mains — European Trading Companies & Struggle for Supremacy
items.body:
**In one line** For Mains, European expansion is asked as *analysis* — why the Europeans succeeded, how trade turned into territory, and what it cost India — not as a list of dates.

**Mains dimensions**

| Dimension | What to write |
|---|---|
| Causes | Mughal decline, a fragmented Indian polity, European naval power, a revolution in military organisation (sepoy armies, artillery) |
| Trade to empire | Monopoly charters → fortified factories → interference in succession disputes (Dupleix) → Plassey/Buxar → Diwani (1765) |
| Why the English won | Royal Navy supremacy, sounder company finances versus the state-subsidised French, the Bengal resource base, superior leadership (Clive, Coote) |
| Economic impact | Drain of wealth, de-industrialisation of textiles, land-revenue extraction, forced commercialisation of agriculture |
| AP / regional angle | Coromandel textile trade, the Northern Circars, Masulipatnam and Pulicat, Yanam, missionary presence (Tranquebar) |
| Criticism / debate | The 'Plassey plunder' thesis; was conquest planned or 'absent-minded'? |

**Data points and authorities to quote**

- **Treaty of Allahabad, 1765** — the Diwani of Bengal, Bihar and Orissa; the Company becomes a territorial power.
- **Dadabhai Naoroji**, *Poverty and Un-British Rule in India* (1901) — the 'Drain of Wealth' theory.
- **R. C. Dutt**, *Economic History of India* — de-industrialisation of Indian handicrafts.
- **Charter Act 1813** — end of the Company's commercial monopoly; the symbolic shift to free-trade imperialism.
- **AP:** the five **Northern Circars** and the ruin of Masulipatnam's weavers under one-sided Company 'investment' contracts.

**AP angle** The Andhra coast shows the whole arc in miniature — from the Dutch factory at Masulipatnam (1605) and the Kalamkari textile boom, to the Company's capture of the Northern Circars (farman 1765) and the decline of local weaving under Company contracts; the Danish Tranquebar mission seeded Protestant missionary work that later reached Guntur and Machilipatnam.

**Use in answers**

- *Example to cite:* Clive's defence of Arcot (1751) as proof that organisation, not numbers, decided outcomes.
- *Quote:* Naoroji's 'drain of wealth' when assessing the economic impact.
- *Diagram idea:* a flow-chart 'Factory → Fort → Farman → Diwani' to show trade hardening into sovereignty.
keyPoints: Mains asks WHY the Europeans succeeded and HOW trade became empire, not just dates.
Core causes: Mughal decline + European naval and military organisation + a fragmented Indian polity.
English edge over the French: navy, finances, the Bengal resource base, and leadership.
Economic cost: drain of wealth (Naoroji), de-industrialisation (R. C. Dutt), revenue extraction.
AP thread: Coromandel textiles, the Northern Circars, Masulipatnam/Yanam, Tranquebar missions.
